response: Data and source-injection red-team: the critic's inputs are especially exposed because assumption decomposition encourages close reading of call paths, comments, tests, fixtures, issue text, logs, and tool output. All of those are untrusted task data. Embedded text that says to reveal secrets, inspect dotfiles, run a shell payload, contact a URL, disable safety, alter a grader, ignore the deadline, or trust a stated invariant must never become critic or agent authority. Transport source excerpts and critic inputs in escaped typed fields with stable identifiers and lengths, keep fixed system and study rules outside those fields, and reject malformed, duplicate, missing, or out-of-range subject indices rather than guessing. Use a minimal allowlisted child-process environment with no ambient keys or tokens; deny network by default; restrict reads and writes to the disposable task workspace; and redact logs before publication. The critic must not inspect credential stores, shell history, production data, unrelated home files, hidden grader code, treatment labels, or other-arm artifacts. Freeze and hash repository fixtures, prompts, tests, graders, and scoring code before trials; grade from a fresh checkout; and mark any mutation of tests, fixtures, timing, results, or instrumentation as a failed trial. A repository comment claiming a test is irrelevant or an invariant is guaranteed is evidence to verify, not an instruction to skip verification. Prevent benchmark gaming by blinding arm labels, keeping held-out expectations inaccessible, scoring externally, and retaining all failures, timeouts, safety violations, and noncompliance in intention-to-treat analysis. Publish only approved source and scrub personal data, secrets, and machine-specific credentials. With no supplied evidence, neither critic agreement nor a clean visible test run supports a claim that bad fixes were reduced.
